'''Maxine Frank Singer''' (née '''Frank'''; February 15, 1931 – July 9, 2024) was an American [[molecular biologist]] and science administrator.<ref name="NLM Profiles Singer">{{cite web |title=Profiles in Science, The Maxine Singer Papers |date=March 12, 2019 |url=https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/206 |publisher=U.S. National Library of Medicine |access-date=November 7, 2015 |archive-date=October 24, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024205408/https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/206 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  She was known for her contributions to solving the [[genetic code]], her role in the ethical and regulatory debates on [[recombinant DNA]] techniques (including the organization of the [[Asilomar Conference on Recombinant DNA]]), and her leadership of [[Carnegie Institution of Washington]].

In 2002, ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'' magazine recognized her as one of the 50 most important women in science.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite magazine|last1=Svitil|first1=Kathy|title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/|access-date=May 1, 2019|magazine=[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]|date=November 13, 2002|archive-date=May 11, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190511023736/http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Maxine Frank was born in New York City to Henrietta and Hyman Frank.<ref name=NYTobit/> Her father was a lawyer, and her mother a homemaker.<ref name=NYTobit/><ref name="Singer Papers, LOC">{{cite web |title=Maxine Singer Papers, 1952–2004 (Biographical Note) |url=http://findingaids.loc.gov/db/search/xq/searchMfer02.xq?_id=loc.mss.eadmss.ms007071&_faSection=overview&_faSubsection=bioghist&_dmdid=d1877e19 |access-date=March 13, 2015 |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402090256/http://findingaids.loc.gov/db/search/xq/searchMfer02.xq?_id=loc.mss.eadmss.ms007071&_faSection=overview&_faSubsection=bioghist&_dmdid=d1877e19 |url-status=live }}</ref>

After attending [[Midwood High School]] in [[Brooklyn]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Putting Science First |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/1989/02/14/putting-science-first/d61aeac0-0fd5-4d7b-8414-2a6654807ae3/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=February 14, 1989 |access-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-date=December 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227191758/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/1989/02/14/putting-science-first/d61aeac0-0fd5-4d7b-8414-2a6654807ae3/ |url-status=live }}</ref> she majored in chemistry and minored in biology at [[Swarthmore College]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://ascb.org/wp-content/uploads/2009/04/Maxine_singer.pdf|title=American Society for Cell Biology Member Profile: Maxine Singer|access-date=March 13, 2015|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402191433/http://ascb.org/wp-content/uploads/2009/04/Maxine_singer.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>  She went on to earn a PhD in 1957 at [[Yale University]], researching [[protein chemistry]] under [[Joseph Fruton]].<ref name=NYTobit/>

== Career ==
After graduating, Fruton encouraged her to specialize in [[nucleic acid]]s, and in 1956 she joined the Laboratory of Biochemistry of [[Leon A. Heppel]] at the [[National Institutes of Health]].<ref name="Singer bio">{{cite web |title=Maxine Singer |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/maxine-singer |website=[[Science History Institute]] |date=June 29, 2016 |access-date=March 21, 2018 |archive-date=March 22, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180322081525/https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/maxine-singer |url-status=live }}</ref>  She led various biochemical research groups as the Chief of the Laboratory of Biochemistry at the National Cancer institute between 1980 and 1987.<ref name=":1"/>

In the wake of the 1973 report of the first use of [[recombinant DNA]] techniques to introduce genes from one species into another, Singer was among the first to call attention to the possible risks of genetic engineering.  She was a chairperson of the 1973 [[Gordon Research Conferences|Gordon Conference]] on Nucleic Acids, where the possible public health risks of the technique were discussed,<ref name="Berg Papers Letter 1973">{{cite web |title=Letter from Maxine Singer to participants in the 1973 Gordon Conference on Nucleic Acids |url=https://www.profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/cd|work=The Paul Berg Papers, U.S. National Library of Medicine|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202020333/https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/CD/B/B/C/F/|archive-date=February 2, 2017}}</ref> and she helped to organize the 1975 [[Asilomar Conference on Recombinant DNA]] that resulted in guidelines for dealing with the largely unknown risks of the technique.<ref name="NLM Profiles Singer" />

Singer was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1978.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web |title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter S |url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterS.pdf |publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |access-date=April 7, 2011 |archive-date=October 5, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005022307/http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterS.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1988, she became president of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, a position she held until 2002.<ref name="Carnegie News">{{cite news |title=Maxine Singer Named President Of Carnegie |url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/8455/title/Maxine-Singer-Named-President-Of-Carnegie/ |work=The Scientist |date=February 23, 1987 |access-date=March 13, 2015 |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402211746/http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/8455/title/Maxine-Singer-Named-President-Of-Carnegie/ |url-status=live }}</ref> She was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1990.<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Maxine+Singer&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=April 19, 2022 |website=search.amphilsoc.org |archive-date=April 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220419135356/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Maxine+Singer&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |url-status=live }}</ref> Singer received the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1992 "for her outstanding scientific accomplishments and her deep concern for the societal responsibility of the scientist"<ref name="NatlMedalSci Singer">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/singer.jsp|title=Maxine F. Singer (1931–) {{!}} The National Medal of Science 50th Anniversary|website=www.nsf.gov}}</ref> and was the first woman to receive the [[Vannevar Bush Award]], in 1999.<ref name="Vannevar Bush Award">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/awards/bush_recipients.jsp#a1999|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191005093348/https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/awards/bush_recipients.jsp#a1999|archive-date=October 5, 2019|title=Vannevar Bush Award Recipients|website=National Science Board}}</ref> In 2007, she was awarded the [[Public Welfare Medal]] from the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Maxine F. Singer to Receive Public Welfare Medal |url=http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=01122007 |agency=National Academy of Sciences |date=January 12, 2007 |access-date=March 13, 2015 |archive-date=March 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150302035707/http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=01122007 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2010, she was awarded the Viktor Hamburger Outstanding Educator Prize from the [[Society for Developmental Biology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Society for Developmental Biology {{!}} Viktor Hamburger Outstanding Educator Prize |url=https://www.sdbonline.org/hamburger_prize |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=www.sdbonline.org}}</ref> 

=== Research contributions ===
Singer made important contributions to the fields of [[biochemistry]] and [[molecular biology]].<ref name=NYTobit/> Her research with Leon Heppel on the role of enzymes that regulate synthesis of nucleic acids played a part in helping [[Marshall Warren Nirenberg|Marshall Nirenberg]] and [[J. Heinrich Matthaei|Heinrick Matthaei]] to decipher the genetic code.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/217|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611152037/http://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/217|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 11, 2011|title=The Maxine Singer Papers: Nucleic Acids, the Genetic Code, and Transposable Genetic Elements: A Life in Research|website=profiles.nlm.nih.gov|access-date=November 7, 2017}}</ref> They studied [[polynucleotide phosphorylase]], an enzyme that can join individual nucleotides into random [[RNA]] sequences. They investigated the base compositions of these polynucleotides using [[electrophoresis]] and [[paper chromatography]], which enabled them to understand how the enzyme catalyzed their synthesis.<ref name=":0" /> These experiments allowed them to create a library of artificial RNA strands with defined sequences, such as a molecule made of only triplets of [[uracil]] that would code for [[phenylalanine]]. These artificial polynucleotides were used by Nirenberg to support the hypothesis that RNA plays a key role in the synthesis of proteins using information from DNA. The RNA sequences that Singer produced were used to match each of the twenty amino acids to a different RNA nucleotide triplet.<ref name=":0" />

[[File:Maxine Singer, Ph.D. (33103348331).jpg|thumb|right|200px|Singer in 1956]]
Singer's research included the study of [[chromatin]] structure and [[genetic recombination]] of viruses. During her time as the head of the Laboratory of Biochemistry at the National Cancer Institute in the 1980s, her research focused on LINEs, or [[long interspersed nucleotide elements]].<ref name=":0" /> She focused on LINE-1, a [[retrotransposon]] found in mammalian genomes that is scattered in thousands of places in the human genome, which she concluded is capable of movement and insertion into new places in the chromosomal DNA.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hohjoh|first1=Hirohiko|last2=Singer|first2=Maxine F.|date=October 1, 1997|title=Sequence-specific single-strand RNA binding protein encoded by the human LINE-1 retrotransposon|journal=The EMBO Journal|language=en|volume=16|issue=19|pages=6034–6043|doi=10.1093/emboj/16.19.6034|issn=0261-4189|pmid=9312060|pmc=1170233}}</ref> She studied the mechanism of how LINE-1 replicates and disperses copies to new locations in the genome, and found that the insertion of these elements could induce mutations in nearby genes, playing a role in genetic disease.<ref name=":0" />

=== Contributions to scientific community ===
Besides her scientific research, Singer was influential in refining science policy.<ref name=NYTobit/> When she was the co-chair of the [[Gordon Research Conferences|Gordon Conference]] in 1973, she raised concerns over the potential health effects and risks in the relatively new field of [[recombinant DNA technology]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.aacc.org/community/awards/hall-of-fame/bios/l-to-s/maxine-singer.aspx|title=Maxine Singer|website=www.aacc.org|access-date=November 7, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029140041/https://www.aacc.org/community/awards/hall-of-fame/bios/l-to-s/maxine-singer.aspx|archive-date=October 29, 2019}}</ref> She organized the 1975 [[Asilomar Conference on Recombinant DNA|Asilomar conference]] in order to bring together scientists to impose restrictions and draw guidelines on recombinant DNA research, where she recommended resumption of research under cautious safeguards until more was known about the potential biohazards of recombinant DNA technology.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Singer|first1=M.|last2=Berg|first2=P.|date=July 16, 1976|title=Recombinant DNA: NIH Guidelines|journal=Science|language=en|volume=193|issue=4249|pages=186–188|doi=10.1126/science.11643320|issn=0036-8075|pmid=11643320|bibcode=1976Sci...193..186S}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/206|title=The Maxine Singer Papers: Biographical Information|website=profiles.nlm.nih.gov|access-date=October 24, 2017|archive-date=October 24, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024205408/https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/ps/retrieve/Narrative/DJ/p-nid/206|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Singer was also an advocate for women and inclusivity in science.<ref>{{Cite Q|Q130287086}}</ref> She wrote an editorial in ''Science'' arguing that universities should encourage women pursuing science and engineering rather than wasting their skills due to unintentional bias against them.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Singer|first=Maxine|date=November 10, 2006|title=Beyond Bias and Barriers|journal=Science|language=en|volume=314|issue=5801|pages=893|doi=10.1126/science.1135744|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17095660|doi-access=}}</ref> Singer also introduced the "First Light" project, a science education program for elementary school students in Washington, D.C. aiming to improve mathematics and science education in schools.<ref name=":1" />

Singer wrote over 100 scientific papers, and also published several books with co-author Paul Berg intended to help the public have a better understanding of molecular genetics, including ''Genes and Genomes'' (1991), ''Dealing with Genes'' (1993), and ''George Beadle: An Uncommon Farmer'' (2003).<ref name=":2" /> In 2018 she published ''Blossoms: And the Genes that Make Them,'' which describes the genetic and evolutionary reasons that flowers bloom.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/blossoms-9780198811138?cc=us&lang=en&|title=Blossoms: And the Genes That Make Them|date=June 5, 2018|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-881113-8|location=Oxford, New York|access-date=October 15, 2020|archive-date=February 8, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220208001638/https://global.oup.com/academic/product/blossoms-9780198811138?cc=us&lang=en&|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Maxine married Daniel Singer, a Swarthmore classmate and political science major, in 1952.<ref name=obit/><ref name=NYTobit/> They had four children: Ellen, [[Amy Singer (historian)|Amy]], David, and [[Stephanie Singer|Stephanie]].<ref>{{cite news |date=May 31, 1993 |title=Weddings: Stephanie Singer, Stephen Fischer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/05/31/style/weddings-stephanie-singer-stephen-fischer.html |work=The New York Times |access-date=June 9, 2024 |archive-date=June 9, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609203730/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/05/31/style/weddings-stephanie-singer-stephen-fischer.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=NYTobit/>

Singer died from [[chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]] and [[emphysema]] at her home in Washington, D.C., on July 9, 2024, at the age of 93.<ref name=obit>{{Cite web |date=June 12, 2024 |title=Maxine Singer, renowned biologist and advocate for STEM inclusion, dies at 93 |url=https://carnegiescience.edu/news/maxine-singer-renowned-biologist-and-advocate-stem-inclusion-dies-93 |access-date=July 10, 2024 |website=carnegiescience.edu |language=en |archive-date=July 9, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240709232324/https://carnegiescience.edu/news/maxine-singer-renowned-biologist-and-advocate-stem-inclusion-dies-93 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=NYTobit>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/10/science/maxine-singer-dead.html|title=Maxine Singer, Guiding Force at the Birth of Biotechnology, Dies at 93|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=July 10, 2024|accessdate=July 10, 2024|archive-date=July 10, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240710193133/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/10/science/maxine-singer-dead.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
